title: The history of the bar code V1

parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: The history of the bar code
parts.article:
The history of the bar code
 
(A) The first step toward today’s bar codes came in 1948, when Bernard Silver, a graduate student in the USA, overheard a conversation in the halls of Philadelphia’s Drexel Institute of Technology. The president of a food chain was pleading with a professor to undertake research on a method of capturing product information automatically at store checkouts. The professor turned down the request, but Bernard Silver mentioned the conversation to his friend Norman Woodland, a twenty-seven-year-old teacher at Drexel. The problem fascinated the two friends, and they set about thinking of a solution. Their first idea was to use patterns printed with an ink that would glow under ultraviolet light, and they built a device to test the concept. It worked, but the printing costs were high and the patterns faded over time. Nonetheless, they were convinced they had a workable idea. After several months of work they came up with the linear bar code, using elements from two established technologies: Morse code, in which letters and numbers are coded into a system of dots and dashes, and the method used to record soundtracks in movies. Silver and Woodland patented the idea in 1952, describing their invention as ‘article classification… through the medium of identifying patterns’. But the cost, together with the fact that their scanning equipment was rather unreliable, made the idea a non-starter at that time.
 
(B) Scanning systems made little progress until the 1970s, when lasers became affordable. Following this, various systems came into use around the world in stores, libraries, factories, and the like, each with its own proprietary code, but there was no standardization. A consortium of grocery manufacturers and retailers therefore set up a committee to look into bar codes, and to standardize what became known formally as the Universal Product Code (UPC). At the heart of the committee’s guidelines were a few basic principles. To make life easier for the cashier, bar codes would have to be readable from almost any angle and at a range of distances. Because they would be reproduced by the million, the labels would have to be cheap and easy to print. And to be affordable, automated checkout systems would have to pay for themselves in two and a half years. The committee considered more than a dozen versions of bar codes, including one based on multi-colored dots and another using a circular bull’s-eye design with lines radiating from a central point. On April 1, 1973, they unanimously agreed on a standardized UPC, a combination of black and white lines and numbers, based on Woodland and Silver’s idea but developed by George Laurer at IBM. Alan Haberman, who headed the subcommittee as president of First National Stores, described the bar code as a kind of world language that worked for everyone. He recalls proudly, ‘We showed that it could be done on a massive scale, that cooperation… was possible for the common good, and that business didn’t need the government to shove them in the right direction.’
 
(C) The investment involved in the bar-code revolution was huge. Each of the tens of thousands of grocery outlets in the US had to spend at least $200,000 on new scanning equipment. Chains had to install new data processing centers and retrain their employees. Printers had to develop the new types of ink, plates, and other technology to reproduce the code with the exact tolerances it requires, and manufacturers had to spend millions of dollars a year on the labels. On June 26, 1974, all the tests were done, all the proposals were complete, all the standards were set, and at a supermarket in Ohio, a single pack of Juicy Fruit chewing gum became the first retail product sold with the help of a bar code scanner. Decades of schemes and billions of dollars in investment now became a practical reality. The bar code on any product could be read and understood in every suitably equipped store.
 
(D) The advantages of the system were not clear immediately, as wholesalers, retailers and customers remained suspicious. Some customers believed bar codes were a form of surveillance. During the early weeks, Business Week magazine ran the headline ‘The Supermarket Scanner That Failed’. However, the benefits eventually became apparent. ‘It turns out there were massive savings in labor and other areas,’ Haberman says. These included checking out items at twice the speed compared to using traditional equipment, which meant shorter lines. And it did not take supermarkets too long to see that, as well as vastly improving customer service, the bar code could hugely reduce the amount of time spent checking inventory.
 
(E) Now, every day more than 5 billion bar codes are scanned in retail outlets throughout the world. Passengers’ luggage is tagged with bar codes by airlines. Staff attach them to babies to ensure the right babies go home from hospitals with the right mothers. Runners in major marathons set off with bar codes on their vests, and librarians rely on them. Tiny bar codes have even been mounted on bees by researchers to track their movements. As for that original pack of Juicy Fruit, it is now, unchewed and unopened, in the Smithsonian Institution National Museum of American History in Washington.

analyses.content: 题目中的 “special type of” 对应原文的 “patterns printed with an...”，核心名词是 ink。
(Paragraph A) “Their first idea was to use patterns printed with an ink that would glow under ultraviolet light...”
题目说第一套系统使用紫外线和一种特殊类型的____，原文A段提到他们最初的想法是使用一种能在紫外线下发光的“ink（墨水）”，填 ink。
题目说基于摩斯密码和用于电影____的技术，原文A段提到该方法也被用于记录电影中的“soundtracks（原声/声轨）”，填 soundtracks。
题目中的 “films” 对应原文的 “movies”，注意要填复数，因为原文是 soundtracks。
(Paragraph A) “...and the method used to record soundtracks in movies.”
题目问第二套系统的问题：____且昂贵。原文A段说扫描设备相当“unreliable（不可靠）”，且成本高，填 unreliable。
题目用 “and” 连接了两个形容词，原文是 “together with the fact that... was rather unreliable”，对应 costly/expensive。
(Paragraph A) “But the cost, together with the fact that their scanning equipment was rather unreliable, made the idea a non-starter...”
“Cheaper” 对应原文的 “affordable”，填造成这一变化的核心技术名词。
题目说1970年代更便宜的____的出现意味着扫描技术传播更广，原文B段开头说直到1970年代“lasers（激光）”变得负担得起（affordable），填 lasers。
(Paragraph B) “Scanning systems made little progress until the 1970s, when lasers became affordable.”
题目说问题在于代码系统缺乏____，原文B段说虽然有各种系统，但没有“standardization（标准化）”，填 standardization。
“Lack of” 对应原文的 “there was no...”。
(Paragraph B) “...each with its own proprietary code, but there was no standardization.”
题目说结账的____增加了，原文D段提到以两倍的“speed（速度）”结账，填 speed。
“Checking out items” 对应题目 “checkouts”，两倍速度即速度增加（increased）。
(Paragraph D) “These included checking out items at twice the speed compared to using traditional equipment...”
(Paragraph E) “Runners in major marathons set off with bar codes on their vests...”
“Participants” 对应原文的 “Runners”，题目结构是 “participants in ______”，所以填活动名称。
题目说现在的用户包括____的参与者，原文E段提到大型“marathons（马拉松）”的跑步者（runners），填 marathons。
题目说科学家正在研究____，原文E段提到微型条形码甚至被研究人员安装在“bees（蜜蜂）”身上，填 bees。
“Scientists studying” 对应原文的 “researchers to track...”，被研究对象是 bees。
(Paragraph E) “Tiny bar codes have even been mounted on bees by researchers to track their movements.”

groups.description:
Complete the notes below.
Write ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 1–8 on your answer sheet.

questions.question: Bernard Silver was invited to develop a system for capturing product information by the president of a food chain.

analyses.content: 题目说Bernard Silver是被食品连锁店总裁“邀请（invited）”去开发系统的。原文A段说是总裁请求一位“教授（professor）”，而Silver只是“无意中听到（overheard）”了对话，选 FALSE。
张冠李戴，被邀请的是教授，Silver只是旁听者。
(Paragraph A) “The president of a food chain was pleading with a professor to undertake research... but Bernard Silver overheard a conversation...”

questions.question: A committee set up in the 1970s said bar codes should be easy to use and not too expensive.

analyses.content: (Paragraph B) “To make life easier for the cashier... labels would have to be cheap and easy to print.”
题目说1970年代成立的委员会说条形码应该易于使用且不太贵。原文B段提到方针是：标签必须“cheap（便宜）”且易于打印，对收银员来说“readble（易读/易用）”，选 TRUE。
“Easy to use” 对应 “make life easier for the cashier / readable”，“not too expensive” 对应 “cheap”。

questions.question: Alan Haberman disagreed with government policies on business matters.

analyses.content: 题目说Alan Haberman不同意政府的商业政策。原文B段末尾他只是自豪地说商业“不需要政府推动（didn't need government to shove）”，并没有提到他反对具体的“policies（政策）”，选 NOT GIVEN。
“不需要帮助”不等于“反对政策”，文中没有关于他对具体政策看法的描述。
(Paragraph B) “...business didn’t need the government to shove them in the right direction.”

questions.question: Many grocery outlets were unable to afford the necessary scanning equipment.

analyses.content: 题目说许多杂货店“买不起（unable to afford）”扫描设备。原文C段只说投资巨大，每家店“不得不花费（had to spend）”20万美元，但没说它们买不起，反而后文说这成了现实，选 NOT GIVEN。
“Expensive（昂贵）” 不等于 “Unaffordable（买不起）”，不要过度推断。
(Paragraph C) “Each of the tens of thousands of grocery outlets in the US had to spend at least $200,000...”

questions.question: The advantages of the new bar code scanner took some time to be accepted by users.

analyses.content: 题目说新条形码扫描仪的优势“花了一段时间（took some time）”才被用户接受。原文D段说优势“并非通过立刻显现（not clear immediately）”，顾客保持“怀疑（suspicious）”，直到最终变得明显，选 TRUE。
“Not clear immediately” 和 “eventually became apparent” 都在强调这是一个耗时的过程。
(Paragraph D) “The advantages of the system were not clear immediately, as wholesalers, retailers and customers remained suspicious... However, the benefits eventually became apparent.”
